title: Windowing Strategies
summary: An unbounded stream can't be aggregated as a whole — you have to cut it into finite chunks first. Tumbling, sliding, and session windows are the three shapes that cut, each fitting a different question.

slides.markdown:
"Average order value" is meaningless over an unbounded stream — average of what, over what period? A **window** is the answer: a finite slice of the stream that an aggregation runs over, so "average" has a concrete denominator.

The [previous topic](event-time-watermarks) covered *when* a window is considered done. This one covers *what shape* the window is in the first place — the three standard shapes (tumbling, sliding, session) cover the overwhelming majority of real streaming metrics, and picking the wrong one either produces the wrong number or an unnecessarily expensive pipeline.

By the end, you should be able to look at a metric definition — "5-minute QPS," "per-user session revenue" — and immediately know which window shape it implies.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you must window before aggregating
slides.markdown:
A `SUM` or `COUNT` over an unbounded stream has no defined end, so it can never emit a final answer — it would just keep running forever, one number that's always "as of right now."

Windowing solves this by carving the stream into finite groups the aggregation can actually close over: "sum of orders **in this 5-minute slice**" has a clear start, end, and therefore a clear moment to emit a result. Without a window boundary, "aggregate this stream" isn't a well-formed question — you have to answer "aggregate over what subset" first.

Every aggregation you'll see in a streaming system — count, sum, average, top-K, distinct — is really "this aggregation, over this window." The window is not optional scaffolding around the aggregation; it's the thing that makes the aggregation well-defined at all.

The three standard window shapes, drawn on the same event timeline, look visibly different in how their boundaries relate to each other:

- **Tumbling** — fixed-size, back-to-back, never overlapping. Every event belongs to exactly one window.
- **Sliding** — fixed-size, but a new window starts before the previous one ends. Events near the boundary belong to multiple windows at once.
- **Session** — no fixed size at all; a window's boundary is defined by a gap of inactivity, so window length varies per session.

slides.subTitle: Fixed, non-overlapping
slides.markdown:
A **tumbling window** splits the stream into fixed-length, back-to-back intervals — every event falls into exactly one window, with no overlap and no gap between windows.

This is the natural fit whenever the metric itself implies a fixed reporting period: "orders per minute," "error count per 5-minute bucket," "hourly active users." Each window produces exactly one independent number, and that number never needs to be reconciled against a neighboring window's result — a clean, simple mental model.

The trade-off: because windows don't overlap, you only get one data point per window duration. If you want to see "orders per minute" update every 10 seconds instead of jumping once a minute, tumbling windows can't do that — that's what sliding windows are for.

slides.subTitle: Overlap, and its cost
slides.markdown:
A **sliding window** has a fixed length, like a tumbling window, but a new window starts at a shorter interval — the **slide** — than the window's length. A 5-minute window with a 1-minute slide produces a new result every minute, each covering the trailing 5 minutes.

This gives you a smoother, more frequently updated view of the same underlying metric — useful for anomaly detection, where you want to catch a spike quickly rather than waiting for a whole tumbling period to elapse.

The cost is real: each event now belongs to `window_length / slide_interval` windows at once (5 windows, for the example above), so both the state the engine maintains and the number of results it emits multiply by that same factor compared to a tumbling window. Smoother output is not free — it's a direct multiplier on compute and storage cost.

slides.subTitle: Gap-based, activity-driven
slides.markdown:
A **session window** has no fixed length at all. Instead, a session stays open as long as events keep arriving within some maximum gap of each other, and closes the moment that gap is exceeded — the window's actual length is whatever the activity pattern produces.

This fits data that's naturally bursty per entity: a user's browsing session, a device's active-use period, a support conversation. "Per-session revenue" or "per-session page views" only makes sense against activity-defined boundaries — a fixed 10-minute tumbling window would arbitrarily split one continuous browsing session into two, or merge two genuinely separate visits into one.

Session windows are typically **keyed** — each user or device gets its own independent sequence of sessions, opening and closing on its own schedule, unlike tumbling and sliding windows which usually share the same boundaries across all keys.

A typical session-window aggregation, grouping clicks into user sessions with a 30-minute inactivity gap:

```sql
SELECT
  user_id,
  SESSION_START(30, 'MINUTE')  AS session_start,
  SESSION_END(30, 'MINUTE')    AS session_end,
  COUNT(*)                     AS clicks_in_session,
  SUM(revenue)                 AS session_revenue
FROM clicks
GROUP BY
  user_id,
  SESSION(event_time, INTERVAL '30' MINUTE)
```

Every row for a given `user_id` that arrives within 30 minutes of the previous one gets folded into the same session; a 31-minute gap closes the current session and starts a new one on the next event. The session's actual duration — 2 minutes or 2 hours — falls out of the data, not out of a config value, which is exactly the property tumbling and sliding windows don't have.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a window for a metric
slides.subTitle: 5-min QPS vs per-session revenue
slides.markdown:
Two concrete metrics, two different correct answers:

| Metric | Right window | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Queries per second, reported every 5 minutes | Tumbling, 5-minute | The metric's own definition is a fixed period; no overlap needed, no activity boundary involved |
| A smoothed "requests/sec, updated every 10 seconds" | Sliding, e.g. 1-minute window / 10-second slide | Needs frequent updates over a longer trailing window — tumbling can't update faster than its own length |
| Revenue per user session | Session, e.g. 30-minute gap | The metric is defined by user activity, not a clock; a fixed window would cut sessions arbitrarily |

The general rule: if the metric's definition names a clock period, reach for tumbling (or sliding, if it also needs frequent updates). If the metric's definition names an *entity's activity*, reach for session. Picking based on "which one is easiest to implement" instead of matching the metric's own definition is how you end up reporting a technically-computed but semantically wrong number.

A team wants a smoother chart and shrinks a 10-minute sliding window's slide from 1 minute to 5 seconds — a 120x increase in how often results are computed and emitted for the exact same underlying window length.

Both the compute cost (recomputing the aggregate on every slide) and the result volume (one output row per slide, per key) scale directly with how much smaller the slide gets relative to the window length. At extreme ratios, the pipeline can spend more resources emitting near-duplicate results than it spends on the aggregation logic itself — and the downstream consumer, whether a dashboard or a database, now has to absorb that same 120x write volume.

The fix is almost never "more compute" — it's asking whether the consumer actually needs sub-10-second granularity, or whether a coarser slide (or even a tumbling window) would serve the same purpose at a fraction of the cost.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
The three shapes above are all time-based, but not every windowing need is. Two variants worth knowing:

- **Global windows** — the entire stream is treated as one window with no automatic close; you supply your own trigger (a count, an external signal) to decide when to emit. This is the fallback when neither time nor a gap defines your boundary — for example, "emit a result every 1,000 events" regardless of how long that takes.
- **Count-based windows** — closes after a fixed number of events rather than a fixed duration, useful when the *rate* of the stream is irrelevant and only the *volume* matters, like batching exactly 500 records per downstream write regardless of how fast they arrive.

Interviewers who go beyond "name the three window types" are usually probing whether you know windowing doesn't have to be time-based at all — the boundary just has to be *some* well-defined trigger, and time is merely the most common one.

A window shape alone doesn't tell you *when* to emit — that's still the watermark's job from the previous topic. The two combine: the window defines *what data goes together*, the watermark defines *when that group is probably complete*.

A 5-minute tumbling window with a 30-second watermark slack fires roughly 30 seconds after its end boundary. A session window closes only once the watermark passes the configured inactivity gap past the last event seen for that key — so a session's watermark-driven close time is itself variable, exactly like the session's length.

The next topic, Stateful Stream Processing, covers what an engine actually has to keep in memory or on disk to make any of this work — the state backing every open window until it closes.
